newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SOCCER-NO IRREGULARITIES IN KANU TRANSFER, FIFA SAY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-NO IRREGULARITIES IN KANU TRANSFER, FIFA SAY.

text.p: There were no irregularities in the transfer of Nwankwo Kanu from Ajax Amsterdam to Inter Milan even though the player was found to have a heart defect shortly after joining the Italian club, FIFA said on Wednesday.

"The committee is of the opinion that the responsibility for establishing a player's state of health lay with the purchasing club before conclusion of the contract," FIFA's medical commission said in a statement.
Inter have attempted to declare the transfer and the Nigerian striker's contract void because of his condition.

The 20-year-old Kanu moved from Ajax to Inter for a reported fee of around $2 million in the close-season after playing for the Dutch side as a substitute in last season's European Cup final against Juventus in Rome, which Juventus won on a penalty shoot-out.
He won an Olympic gold medal in August as part of the Nigerian team that beat Argentina in the soccer final in Athens, Georgia.
The transfer was hailed as a coup by Inter but on September 3, before Kanu had played a competitive match in Inter's blue and black stripes, tests revealed a heart-valve problem.
Kanu said he was "emotionally shattered" by the news and a medical report by doctors who advised him to quit playing.
Kanu has since sought further medical advice and is due to undergo heart surgery in the United States next week.
FIFA's medical commission also said on Wednesday that all 34 doping tests carried out at the Atlanta Olympic soccer tournaments for both men and women were negative.
Among matters discussed by FIFA's technical committee on Wednesday was a move to establish a universal and official definition of an own goal.

At present some countries, such as Italy, declare an own goal if the ball touches a defending player, even slightly, on its way into the net, while in England balls that take deflections off defenders are usually credited as a goal to the last attacking player to touch the ball.

The technical committee also hinted that it was divided over a proposal from the referee's committee, which met on Tuesday, to outlaw deliberate backpasses to the goalkeeper with any part of the body.
That matter will be discussed further when the Task Force 2000 think-tank, which is considering the game's future, meets on Friday.
